questions.q: what part had Hamilcar played in Carthage’s earlier war with Rome?
points: he was Carthage’s leading general / commander in the First Punic War

questions.q: what comparison does Nepos make between Hannibal and the Roman people?
points: the Roman people surpassed all nations
in courage / bravery
no one doubts this
Hannibal surpassed all other generals
in skill / intelligence / good judgement
by as much as Rome surpassed all nations (in bravery)
this cannot be denied
questions.guidance: Accept any four. The two halves of the comparison may be credited separately.

questions.q: what claim does Nepos make about Hannibal’s battles in Italy?
points: whenever / every time he fought the Romans in Italy
he always came away the winner

questions.q: why, according to Nepos, did Hannibal fail to defeat the Romans?
points: he was weakened at home
by the jealousy / envy of his own citizens
the criticism / disparagement of many people
overcame the courage / ability of one man

questions.q: how does Nepos make this sentence a striking summary of Hannibal’s fate?
points: contrast / antithesis of multorum (many) and unius (one)
contrast of obtrectatio (spiteful criticism) with virtutem (courage / excellence)
devicit: a military word for ‘utterly defeated’, used of political spite, so Hannibal is beaten by his own people
brevity / a short, pointed sentence after the long ones before it
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what do we learn about Hannibal’s hatred of Rome?
points: it was his father’s hatred
handed down to him like an inheritance
he kept it all his life
he would sooner give up his life than his hatred
even when he had been driven from his homeland
and depended on the resources of others
he never stopped fighting Rome, at least in spirit / in his mind

questions.q: to whom did Hannibal go after he had been driven out of Carthage?
points: King Antiochus (III) / the Seleucid king
questions.guidance: Accept ‘to the king of Syria’ or ‘to the East’ if Antiochus is clearly meant.

questions.q: who was Philip, and how had Hannibal made him an enemy of Rome?
points: king of Macedon (Philip V)
Hannibal made an alliance with him (after Cannae / in 215 BC)
without ever meeting him / from a distance (absens)
questions.guidance: One mark for Philip’s identity; one for either of the other points.

questions.q: what do we learn about Antiochus and about Hannibal’s influence on him?
points: Antiochus was the most powerful king of all at that time
Hannibal fired him with a great desire
for war
so that he tried to bring an army against Italy
all the way from the Red Sea

questions.q: what were the Roman envoys trying to do at the court of Antiochus?
points: find out the king’s intentions / attitude
work through secret plots
make the king suspicious of Hannibal
as if Hannibal had been bribed by the Romans
and now thought differently from before

questions.lemma: neque id frustra … adiit ad regem
questions.q: what happened as a result of the envoys’ efforts, and how did Hannibal react?
points: their plan worked / was not in vain
Hannibal found out about it
he saw that he was being shut out of the king’s inner counsels
he went to the king when the opportunity arose

questions.q: how does Nepos make the Romans’ methods sound underhand?
points: alliteration of the hard c binds ‘plans’ and ‘secret’ together
clandestinis: their plans are hidden / secret, unlike Hannibal’s open loyalty
the plotting is in contrast with Hannibal’s open reminder of his fides
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what details does Hannibal give about the occasion when his father sacrificed?
points: it was his father Hamilcar
Hannibal was a small boy
no more than nine years old
Hamilcar was setting out for Spain
from Carthage
as commander-in-chief
he sacrificed victims
to Jupiter (Best and Greatest)

questions.q: why do you think Hannibal describes himself in this way?
points: the diminutive puerulo stresses how very young he was
so his hatred of Rome was rooted in him before he could choose it / has shaped his whole life
so the king is more likely to trust that his loyalty is lifelong

questions.q: what did Hamilcar ask Hannibal, and when?
points: while the sacrifice / sacred rite was taking place
whether he wanted to go with him to the camp

questions.q: how did the young Hannibal respond, and what condition did Hamilcar set?
points: he accepted gladly
he began to beg his father not to hesitate to take him
Hamilcar said he would do so
if Hannibal gave him the pledge / promise that he demanded

questions.q: describe how the oath was taken.
points: Hamilcar at once led Hannibal to the altar
where he had begun to sacrifice
everyone else was sent away
Hannibal held / touched the altar
he swore that he would never be a friend to the Romans

questions.q: what does Hannibal claim about the way he has kept his oath?
points: he has kept the oath he gave his father
right up to this time of his life
so no one should doubt
that he will be of the same mind for the rest of his life

questions.q: what advice does Hannibal give Antiochus?
points: if he is planning anything friendly towards Rome
he will be wise to hide it from Hannibal
when he is preparing for war
he will cheat himself if he does not put Hannibal in command

questions.q: why do you think Hannibal expresses his advice in this way?
points: litotes / understatement (‘not unwisely’)
it is polite / tactful when speaking to a king
it lets him warn Antiochus without sounding like a threat

questions.q: what do we learn here about the start of Hannibal’s career?
points: he was (about) nine years old
he went to Spain
with his father

questions.q: who was this Hasdrubal?
points: Hamilcar’s son-in-law (who took over the command in Spain after Hamilcar’s death)

questions.q: how did Hannibal come to hold the supreme command?
points: after Hamilcar’s death Hasdrubal took over as commander
Hannibal was put in charge of all the cavalry
when Hasdrubal too was killed
the army gave Hannibal the supreme command
this was publicly approved
when the news reached Carthage

questions.q: what did Hannibal achieve in his first years as commander?
points: he became commander when not yet twenty-five
within the next three years
he conquered all the peoples of Spain in war
he took Saguntum by force / by storm
a city allied to Rome
he raised three very large armies

questions.q: why was Hannibal’s attack on this city so significant?
points: Saguntum was an ally of Rome / on friendly terms with Rome
so attacking it was an act of war against Rome
the siege led directly to the Second Punic War

questions.q: what did Hannibal do with his three armies?
points: he sent one to Africa
he left the second in Spain with his brother Hasdrubal
he led the third into Italy himself

questions.q: what happened on Hannibal’s march towards the Alps?
points: he crossed the pass over the Pyrenees
wherever he went he fought all the inhabitants
he let no one go unless they had been defeated

questions.q: what does Nepos tell us about the Alps?
points: they separate Italy from Gaul
no one had ever crossed them with an army before Hannibal
except the Greek Hercules
because of this the pass is still called the Graian Pass today

questions.q: what did Hannibal do in order to cross the Alps?
points: he cut down the Alpine tribes
who were trying to stop him crossing
he opened up the terrain / cleared the ground
he built roads

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise the scale of Hannibal’s achievement?
points: contrast between elephantus ornatus (a huge, fully laden elephant) and unus homo inermis (a single unarmed man)
repere (‘crawl’) pictures the path as almost impassable before Hannibal’s work
vix (‘barely’) stresses how hard the route had been
ea … qua antea: the same route is shown before and after Hannibal transformed it
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: who was this Scipio?
points: the consul of 218 BC
the father of Scipio Africanus, who later defeated Hannibal at Zama

questions.q: what happened in Hannibal’s first two encounters with Scipio?
points: he fought Scipio at the Rhone
and drove him back
he fought the same man again at Clastidium on the Po
he sent him away wounded
and put to flight / routed

questions.q: describe what happened at the Trebia.
points: Scipio came against Hannibal a third time
together with his colleague Tiberius Longus
Hannibal engaged them both
and crushed them both

questions.q: what happened to Hannibal on his way to Etruria?
points: he crossed the Apennines through the land of the Ligurians
he was struck by a severe disease of the eyes
afterwards he never had the full use of his right eye again

questions.q: what did Hannibal achieve in spite of his illness?
points: while still suffering from the illness
and being carried in a litter
he trapped the consul Flaminius at Lake Trasimene by an ambush
and killed him together with his army
not long afterwards he killed the praetor Centenius
who was holding the mountain passes with picked troops

questions.q: why do you think Nepos includes this detail?
points: the great general is too ill even to walk or ride
so his victory over a consul and his army seems all the more remarkable
it shows that Hannibal wins by his mind / cunning, not his physical strength
it makes him seem human / evokes sympathy

questions.q: what happened when Hannibal reached Apulia?
points: the two consuls, Terentius and Aemilius, came to meet him
in a single battle
he routed both their armies
he killed the consul Paulus
and several ex-consuls as well
including Servilius Geminus
who had been consul the year before

questions.q: what famous battle took place here?
points: Cannae (216 BC)

questions.q: what did Hannibal do after this battle?
points: he set out for Rome
and no one opposed / resisted him

questions.q: what happened next?
points: Hannibal waited in the hills near Rome
he camped there for several days
as he was going back to Capua
Fabius Maximus, the Roman dictator
blocked his path in the Falernian territory

questions.q: what was Fabius’ strategy against Hannibal?
points: he shadowed / followed Hannibal’s army
he avoided a pitched battle

questions.q: how did Hannibal get out of this situation?
points: he was trapped by the narrowness of the terrain
he got his army out at night
without any loss to his army
he tricked / deceived Fabius, a very cunning commander

questions.q: why do you think Nepos describes Fabius in this way at this point?
points: the superlative callidissimo praises Fabius as the cleverest of commanders
he is praised in the very clause in which he is fooled (dedit verba)
so Hannibal appears even cleverer than the cleverest Roman

questions.lemma: namque obducta nocte … nemo sit ausus
questions.q: describe Hannibal’s trick and its effect on the Romans.
points: under cover of darkness
he tied bundles of twigs to the horns of young cattle
he set them on fire
he sent a great many of these animals out
scattering in all directions
the sudden sight
terrified the Roman army
so that no one dared to go outside the rampart

questions.lemma: hanc post rem … pari modo interfecit
questions.q: what further successes did Hannibal win?
points: not many days later he lured Minucius Rufus into battle by a trick
Minucius was Master of Horse with power equal to the dictator
and Hannibal routed him
he destroyed Gracchus, consul for the second time, in an ambush in Lucania
even though Hannibal himself was not there
he killed Marcellus, five times consul, near Venusia
in the same way (by an ambush)

questions.q: what claims does Nepos make here to show Hannibal’s greatness?
points: it would take too long to list all his battles
as long as he was in Italy no one stood against him in battle
after Cannae no one pitched camp against him in open country

questions.q: what do we learn here about Hannibal’s return to Africa and his new opponent?
points: he left Italy undefeated
he was called home to defend his country
he fought against Publius Scipio
the son of the man
whom Hannibal had already routed three times / at the Rhone, the Po and the Trebia

questions.q: what had this Scipio achieved before he faced Hannibal?
points: he drove the Carthaginians out of Spain
he invaded Africa (in 204 BC)
he was the son of the consul of 218 BC whom Hannibal had beaten
questions.guidance: One mark each for either of the first two points; the third may be credited for one mark.

questions.q: why did Hannibal want to make peace with Scipio?
points: his country’s resources were already exhausted
he wanted to settle the war for the time being
so that he could fight again later from a stronger position

questions.q: how does Nepos make the failure of the talks seem blunt and final?
points: play on words: convenit (the men met) and convenerunt (the terms did not agree)
asyndeton: two short clauses with no connecting word
non placed just before the verb makes the failure stand out
the brevity of the two clauses
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what happened at the battle of Zama and immediately afterwards?
points: a few days after the meeting
he fought the same Scipio at Zama
he was defeated
he reached Hadrumetum
in two days and two nights
a distance of about three hundred miles

questions.q: what happened during the retreat?
points: the Numidians who had left the battle with him
laid an ambush for him
he escaped them
and crushed them as well

questions.q: what did Hannibal do at Hadrumetum?
points: he gathered the survivors of the retreat
he held fresh levies / recruited new troops
within a few days

questions.q: what was Fregellae?

questions.guidance: Accept ‘a town near Rome’ or ‘a Roman colony’.

questions.q: what happened while Hannibal was busy with his preparations?
points: he was preparing (for war) with great energy
the Carthaginians made peace with Rome

questions.q: what did Hannibal and his brother do after the peace was made?
points: Hannibal nevertheless stayed in command of the army
he carried on operations in Africa
his brother Mago did the same
until the consulship of Sulpicius and Aurelius

questions.q: what did the Carthaginian envoys do at Rome, and what did they ask for?

for making peace with them
they presented a golden crown
they asked that their hostages might be kept at Fregellae
they asked for their prisoners to be returned

questions.q: how did the senate reply to the envoys?
points: the gift was welcome and accepted
the hostages could stay where the Carthaginians asked
the prisoners would not be returned
because the Carthaginians still kept Hannibal in command of an army
he was the man responsible for starting the war
he was Rome’s bitterest enemy
his brother Mago was also still in command

questions.q: how does the senate make Hannibal sound especially dangerous?
points: superlative inimicissimum: he is Rome’s very worst enemy
nomini Romano: he is the enemy of the Roman name, everything Rome stands for
it follows straight after he is blamed for starting the war (cuius opera susceptum bellum foret)
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how did the Carthaginians react to the senate’s reply?
points: once they learned of the reply
they recalled Hannibal and Mago home

questions.q: what office did Hannibal hold on his return, and how does Nepos explain it?
points: he was made ‘king’ (suffete) when he returned
after he had been general / praetor
in the twenty-second year (after first becoming general)
it was like the consulship at Rome
two ‘kings’ were elected
every year

questions.q: how did Hannibal behave as a magistrate?
points: he worked with the same energy / diligence
as he had shown in war

questions.q: what did Hannibal achieve with Carthage’s finances?
points: he raised new revenues / taxes
there was enough money
to pay what was owed to Rome under the treaty
there was also a surplus
which was stored in the treasury

questions.q: why might a reader find this detail ironic?
points: Hannibal is Rome’s greatest enemy
yet he now uses his skill to make sure Carthage keeps up its payments to Rome

questions.q: in what year did these men hold the consulship?
points: 196 BC

questions.q: what did Hannibal do when Roman envoys came to Carthage, and why?

questions.lemma: priusquam iis senatus daretur, navem ascendit clam
questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s departure seem sudden and secret?
points: priusquam … daretur: he goes before the envoys can even speak to the senate
clam: he slips away in secret, and the word comes emphatically at the end of the clause
navem ascendit: a short, simple statement of action
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how did the Carthaginians respond to Hannibal’s flight?
points: when it became known
they sent two ships
to arrest him if they could catch him

questions.q: why do you think Nepos includes this detail?

questions.q: where was Cyrene?

questions.guidance: Accept ‘a Greek city in North Africa’.

questions.q: what did Hannibal do in the third year after his flight, and what did he hope to achieve?

with five ships
in the territory of Cyrene

by giving them hope and confidence in Antiochus

to invade Italy with his armies

questions.q: what happened to Mago?
points: Hannibal summoned him to join him there
when the Carthaginians found out

while he was absent / without a hearing

questions.q: what did the brothers do next?
points: their situation was hopeless
they set sail

questions.q: what does Nepos say about Mago’s death?
points: there are two different accounts

questions.q: what does Nepos claim would have happened if Antiochus had listened to Hannibal?

as he had done in starting it

nearer the Tiber / Rome

questions.q: how does Nepos make this comparison effective?
points: antithesis of the two places set side by side
Tiberi: Rome’s own river, at the heart of Roman territory
Thermopylis: a distant pass in Greece
it shows how close Rome came to real danger
questions.guidance: Any two points; at least one must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how did Hannibal serve Antiochus, and how well did he fight?
points: he saw the king attempting many foolish things
yet he never abandoned him
he commanded a few ships
which he had been ordered to bring from Syria to Asia
he fought the fleet of Rhodes in the Pamphylian Sea
his side was beaten by the enemy’s greater numbers
on the wing where he fought, he was victorious

questions.q: why did Hannibal go to Crete, and what did he intend to do there?
points: Antiochus had been defeated / put to flight
he was afraid of being handed over
which would certainly have happened if he had put himself in their power
he went to the Gortynians in Crete
to consider where to go next

questions.q: who were the Gortynians?
points: the people of Gortyn, one of the leading cities of Crete

questions.q: what danger did Hannibal foresee, and why?
points: he would be in great danger
unless he took precautions
because of the greed of the Cretans
he was carrying a large sum of money
he knew that word of it had spread

questions.q: how does Nepos prepare the reader for the story that follows?
points: superlative callidissimus: Hannibal is the shrewdest / most cunning
omnium: of all men, so no one can match him

questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: describe the first part of Hannibal’s plan.
points: he filled several jars
with lead
he covered the tops with gold and silver
he deposited them in the temple of Diana
in front of the leading citizens
pretending to entrust his fortune to their honesty

questions.q: what did Hannibal do with his real money?
points: once the Cretans had been deceived
he filled bronze statues
which he had brought with him
with all his money
he left them lying in the open courtyard of his house

questions.q: how does Nepos show that the plan worked?
points: the Gortynians guarded the temple with great care
against Hannibal more than anyone else

without their knowledge

questions.lemma: non tam a ceteris quam ab Hannibale
questions.q: why is this detail amusing?
points: the temple is guarded against the very man who deposited the treasure
the Cretans are guarding jars of lead
while his real wealth lies in full view in his courtyard

questions.q: why do you think Nepos refers to Hannibal by this name at this point?
points: it means ‘the Phoenician’ / ‘the Carthaginian’
to Romans the word suggested proverbial Punic cunning / trickery
Hannibal has just tricked the Cretans

questions.q: what do we learn about Hannibal’s situation when he reached Prusias?
points: he had saved his fortune / money
he had made fools of the Cretans
all of them
he reached King Prusias
in Pontus

questions.q: how did Hannibal spend his time at the court of Prusias?
points: he kept the same attitude towards Italy
he did nothing else
he armed the king
he trained the king
against the Romans

questions.q: what did Hannibal do, and why?
points: he saw that Prusias lacked the resources to stand on his own / was not strong enough by himself
he won over other kings
he brought warlike nations into alliance with him

questions.lemma: conciliabat ceteros reges, adiungebat bellicosas nationes
questions.q: how does Nepos convey Hannibal’s energy as a diplomat?
points: asyndeton: two clauses with no connecting word
the two clauses are built to match (verb, adjective, noun)
the imperfects conciliabat / adiungebat show continuous, tireless effort
bellicosas: he picks warlike peoples, ready for war with Rome
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what do we learn about Eumenes and his war with Prusias?
points: he was king of Pergamum
he was a very close friend / ally of Rome
he was at odds with Prusias
war was fought between them on land and sea
Eumenes had the advantage on both fronts
because of his alliance with Rome

questions.q: in which part of the world was this king’s kingdom?

questions.q: why was Hannibal so keen to see Eumenes crushed, and what did he do about it?

he thought that if he removed Eumenes
everything else would be easier for him
he devised a plan
to kill him

questions.q: what difficulty did Hannibal face, and how did he decide to deal with it?
points: a sea battle was due within a few days
he was outnumbered in ships
he could not match the enemy in arms / strength
so he would have to fight by trickery

questions.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s use of trickery here?
points: dolo is placed first for emphasis: cunning becomes his weapon
the gerundive of obligation erat pugnandum presents trickery as forced on him by necessity
this excuses a method Romans might think unworthy of a soldier
dolo is contrasted with armis (strength in arms), which he lacks
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what orders did Hannibal give?
points: as many as possible
venomous snakes
alive
were to be collected
and put into earthenware / clay pots

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s weapon seem dangerous?
points: three words pile up the danger
venenatas: they are poisonous
vivas: they are alive
snakes are a strange and startling weapon for a sea battle
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what happened on the day of the battle?
points: Hannibal had collected a great number of snakes
on the very day of the sea battle
he called his marines together
he ordered them all to attack Eumenes’ ship
against the other ships they were only to defend themselves

questions.q: who were these men?
points: marines / soldiers carried on board ship to fight (as distinct from the rowers and sailors)

questions.lemma: omnes ut in unam Eumenis regis concurrant navem
questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s order clear and forceful?
points: juxtaposition of omnes and unam: all against one
hyperbaton: unam … navem frames the king’s name, so the single target stands out

questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what did Hannibal tell his men to encourage them?
points: they would achieve this easily
thanks to the great number of snakes
he would make sure they knew
which ship the king was sailing on
if they captured or killed Eumenes
they would be richly / greatly rewarded

questions.q: what happened before the battle began?
points: after the men had been encouraged
both fleets were led out to battle
the battle lines were drawn up
before the signal was given
Hannibal sent a messenger
in a small boat
with a herald’s staff
so that his men would know where Eumenes was

questions.q: what was this, and how did it help Hannibal’s plan?
points: a herald’s / envoy’s staff
it marked the bearer as sacred / not to be harmed
so it guaranteed the messenger safe passage
it made him look harmless and official
questions.guidance: One mark for identifying it; one for any of the other points.

questions.q: how did the messenger manage to reach Eumenes?
points: he reached the enemy ships
he held up a letter
he said he was looking for the king
he was taken straight to Eumenes
because no one doubted
that the letter contained something about peace

questions.q: why is this phrase ironic?
points: everyone is certain the letter is about peace
the reader knows it is part of Hannibal’s trick
the same words opened the Life (1.1), where the certainty was true; here it is mistaken

questions.q: what did the messenger do next?
points: he pointed out the commander’s / king’s ship to his own side
he went back to where he had come from

questions.q: what did Eumenes find in the letter?
points: when he opened it he found nothing (of importance)

questions.q: how did Eumenes react?
points: he was puzzled about the reason
he could not find an explanation
even so, he did not hesitate
to begin the battle at once

questions.q: who was Eumenes?
points: king of Pergamum
Rome’s chief ally in Asia Minor

questions.q: what did the Bithynians do when the two fleets clashed?
points: they acted on Hannibal’s orders
all of them together
attacked Eumenes’ ship

questions.q: what happened to Eumenes?
points: he could not withstand their attack
he sought safety in flight
he would not have escaped
if he had not taken refuge within his own defences / garrison
which were positioned on the nearby shore

questions.q: what happened to the rest of the Pergamene fleet?
points: they were pressing their opponents hard / harder
suddenly
earthenware / clay pots
began to be thrown onto their ships

questions.q: how did the Pergamenes react to the pots at first, and why?
points: they laughed (at them)
they could not understand why this was being done

questions.q: what made the Pergamenes flee, and what did they do?
points: they saw their ships filled with snakes
they were thoroughly terrified
by this new / unheard-of kind of attack
they could not see which danger to avoid most
they turned their ships round
they went back to their own naval camp

questions.q: how does Nepos convey the panic of the Pergamene sailors?
points: perterriti: the prefix per- intensifies the fear, ‘thoroughly terrified’
nova: the attack is new / unheard of, so nothing had prepared them for it
nova re placed first gives the cause of the panic before the panic itself
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what conclusions does Nepos draw about Hannibal’s abilities?
points: he defeated the Pergamene forces through strategy / cunning
he did so on other occasions too / often
on land / with infantry forces
he drove back his enemies with equal skill / good judgement

questions.q: why is this phrase an effective summary of the episode?
points: antithesis / juxtaposition of consilio (strategy) and arma (weapons)
Hannibal’s brains defeat the enemy’s force of arms
it recalls Nepos’ judgement in chapter 1 that Hannibal excelled in prudentia / good judgement
brevity: two words sum up the whole battle
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: who was Flamininus?
points: Titus Quinctius Flamininus, a former consul (consul in 198 BC)
he defeated Philip V of Macedon (at Cynoscephalae)
he proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks
he led the Roman embassy that came for Hannibal

questions.q: how did the Romans find out where Hannibal was?
points: by chance
envoys of Prusias
were dining in Rome
with (the ex-consul) Flamininus
Hannibal’s name came up in conversation
one of the envoys said that he was in Prusias’ kingdom

questions.q: what did the senate do, and why?
points: Flamininus reported the news to the senate the next day
the senators thought they would never be free from plots
as long as Hannibal was alive
they sent envoys to Bithynia
including Flamininus
to ask the king not to keep their bitterest enemy with him
and to hand him over

questions.q: how did Prusias respond to the Romans’ request?
points: he did not dare to refuse
but he objected to one thing
they should not demand that he himself do something
that was against the laws of hospitality
they should arrest Hannibal themselves, if they could
they would easily find the place where he was

questions.q: what does this phrase suggest about Prusias?
points: litotes / understatement (‘did not dare to refuse’)
he is weak / afraid of Rome
he is too afraid to protect Hannibal, who had served him
questions.guidance: Any two points; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what precautions had Hannibal taken?
points: he stayed in one place
in a fortress / castle
which the king had given him as a gift
he had built it so that it had exits on every side
because he feared what actually happened

questions.q: what happened when the Roman envoys arrived?
points: they surrounded his house
with a large number of men
a boy looking out from the doorway
told Hannibal that more armed men than usual were appearing

questions.q: what did Hannibal order the boy to do?
points: go round all the doors of the building
report back quickly
whether he was surrounded on every side in the same way

questions.q: what did Hannibal realise, and what did he do?
points: the boy reported that every exit was blocked
Hannibal realised that this had not happened by chance
that he himself was the target
that he should no longer keep his life
so as not to lose his life at someone else’s will
remembering his past courage
he took the poison which he always kept with him

questions.q: how does this phrase shape the reader’s view of Hannibal’s death?
points: it presents his suicide as worthy of his past courage / virtutum
it fits the Roman ideal of a noble death
it shows that he keeps control and dies on his own terms
memor: even at the end he remembers who he is

questions.q: what final judgement and facts does Nepos give about Hannibal?
points: he was the bravest of men
he had endured many different hardships
he died / found rest
in his seventieth year

questions.q: why do you think Nepos chose this word to describe Hannibal’s death?
points: it is a euphemism: ‘he found rest’
a gentle word for a death by poison
it suggests peace after a life full of hardship
it gives the Life a calm ending

questions.q: what does Nepos say about the date of Hannibal’s death?
points: there is no agreement about the consuls in whose year he died
Atticus, in his Annals, says the consulship of Marcellus and Fabius Labeo
Polybius says the consulship of Aemilius Paulus and Baebius Tamphilus
Sulpicius Blitho says the consulship of Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus
the dates are given by the names of the consuls
questions.guidance: Accept any four. Names of the consuls need not be complete.

questions.q: who was Atticus?
points: Nepos’ close friend
Cicero’s friend and correspondent
the author of a chronology of Roman history (the Liber Annalis)

essays.q: how does Nepos make this a powerful introduction to Hannibal?
points: Nepos opens like an entry in a list (name, father, nation), at once naming Hamilcar and Carthage
he praises Hannibal as the greatest of all generals, a bold claim for a Roman audience
he protects Roman pride by giving Rome courage and Hannibal skill, so the praise does not insult his readers
Hannibal was never beaten in Italy, and Nepos implies he would have won the war
his downfall is blamed on jealousy at home, which makes him a tragic figure betrayed by his own people
the hatred of Rome is presented as an inheritance from his father, part of his identity
the chapter ends with Hannibal still fighting Rome in spirit even in exile, which sets up the rest of the Life

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a dangerous and determined enemy of Rome?
points: even without being present Hannibal turned Philip of Macedon against Rome
he fired the most powerful king of the age with a desire for war
his influence reached across the whole world, from the Red Sea to Italy
the Romans have to use secret plots against him, which shows how much they fear him
the Romans are shown as sly and deceitful, while Hannibal is open about his loyalty
Hannibal deals with the threat directly, going straight to the king
he goes back to his childhood to prove that his hatred is lifelong and sacred

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s account of his oath persuasive?
points: the story is told in Hannibal’s own words, so it carries his personal authority
the solemn religious setting (the sacrifice, the altar) makes the oath binding before the gods
the boy is eager and pleads to go, so his hatred of Rome seems his own choice as well as his father’s
Hamilcar’s bargain is short and stark, like a contract
the private and physical details (others sent away, hand on the altar) make the scene vivid and believable
Hannibal points to his whole life as proof that he has kept the oath
he ends with tactful but confident advice to the king, asking to be made commander

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as an exceptional commander?
points: Hannibal becomes supreme commander before the age of twenty-five
within three years he conquers all the peoples of Spain
he storms Saguntum, Rome’s ally, a bold act that means war with Rome
he raises three huge armies and plans on a grand scale, sending them to Africa, Spain and Italy
on the march no people he meets escapes defeat
he crosses the Alps, which no army had crossed before except Hercules’, so his feat is placed on the level of legend
he defeats the Alpine tribes and engineers a road where an elephant can pass, which shows practical skill as well as courage

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s victories in Italy seem overwhelming?
points: the same Roman commander, Scipio, is beaten again and again, at the Rhone, the Po and the Trebia
Scipio is sent away wounded and in flight, a humiliating picture of a Roman consul
two consuls together at the Trebia are crushed at once
Hannibal loses the use of an eye, yet wins even while carried in a litter
he destroys Flaminius and his army at Trasimene by an ambush, and soon afterwards Centenius and his picked troops
at Cannae both consular armies are routed in a single battle
the list of the dead rises from a consul to several ex-consuls, showing how much of Rome’s leadership was lost

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as a master of cunning?
points: Hannibal seems trapped by the narrow terrain, yet escapes at night without losing a man
he deceives Fabius, who is described as the cleverest of commanders
the trick with burning branches tied to the horns of cattle is described in vivid detail
the sudden sight terrifies a whole Roman army into staying behind its rampart
he lures Minucius into battle by a trick and routs him
he destroys Gracchus and Marcellus by ambushes, even without being present himself
Nepos ends by claiming no one could face him in open battle, so cunning and strength combine to make him unbeatable in Italy

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal in a positive light even in defeat?
points: he leaves Italy undefeated and is recalled to defend his country, which makes him a patriot
Nepos reminds us that he had beaten Scipio’s father three times
the need for peace is blamed on Carthage’s exhausted resources, not on Hannibal
even his attempt at peace is a plan to fight again later from a stronger position
the defeat at Zama is passed over in a single word
Nepos marvels at his retreat of three hundred miles in two days and nights
he escapes and crushes the Numidians who ambush him
within a few days he has raised a large army again, so the chapter ends with his recovery

essays.q: how does Nepos show the growing gap between Hannibal and his own city?
points: Hannibal throws himself into preparing for war while Carthage makes peace behind his back
he carries on in command regardless, with his brother Mago beside him
Carthage humbly thanks Rome and sends a golden crown, eager to please the victor
the senate’s gracious reply turns into a sharp refusal, and the reason is Hannibal
Rome names him as the man who started the war and its bitterest enemy, so he becomes a problem for Carthage
Carthage obeys at once and recalls its greatest generals, which foreshadows how readily it will abandon him later
even so he is given the highest office in the city, which Nepos explains for his Roman readers

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s fall from power in Carthage seem unjust?
points: Hannibal serves as magistrate with the same energy he showed in war
he puts the finances in order: enough to pay Rome and a surplus for the treasury
Roman envoys arrive, reaching directly into Carthage’s affairs
Hannibal believes they have come to demand his surrender
he flees in secret before they can even be heard
the Carthaginians hunt him with two ships, seize his property and tear down his house
the man who has just filled the treasury is declared an exile by his own city, which recalls the jealousy Nepos blamed in chapter 1

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s loyalty and ability in difficult circumstances?
points: the brothers’ situation is hopeless and they set sail, leaving themselves to fortune
Mago dies an obscure death, by shipwreck or at the hands of his own slaves
Nepos claims that Antiochus would have fought near Rome itself if he had followed Hannibal’s advice
so Hannibal’s strategy is shown to be sound, and the failure is the king’s
Hannibal stays loyal even though he sees the king’s many foolish schemes
he is given only a few ships, which suggests he was undervalued
even in a lost battle he wins on his own wing, which echoes chapter 1, where he always came away the victor

essays.q: how does Nepos make the story of Hannibal’s trick entertaining?
points: Hannibal is introduced as the shrewdest of all men, so the reader expects a clever trick
the Cretans are defined by their greed, so the reader enjoys seeing them outwitted
the trick is simple and clever: jars of lead topped with gold and silver
he deposits them in a temple before the leading citizens, pretending to trust their honesty
his real money is hidden in bronze statues and left lying carelessly in the open
the comic reversal: the Cretans guard the temple against Hannibal himself
the reader knows they are guarding lead while the treasure lies in full view

essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal as an enemy of Rome who never gives up?
points: Hannibal arrives at Prusias’ court fresh from tricking the Cretans, his fortune intact
even in exile his attitude to Italy is unchanged, as Nepos promised in chapter 1
he does nothing else but arm and train the king against Rome
he sees Prusias is too weak alone, so he builds a wider alliance of kings and warlike peoples
Eumenes is Rome’s close friend, so the war with Prusias becomes Hannibal’s war with Rome by proxy
Rome’s alliance gives Eumenes the advantage on land and sea, which only makes Hannibal more determined
he reasons coolly that removing Eumenes will make the rest easier, and plans to kill him

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s preparations for the sea battle interesting?
points: the battle is only days away, which creates urgency
Hannibal is outnumbered and outmatched, so the reader wonders how he can win
he turns to trickery as a necessity
the weapon is extraordinary: as many live, venomous snakes as possible, packed into clay pots
the plan is revealed to the marines only on the day of the battle, which keeps it secret
the orders are simple and clear: all attack the king’s ship and only defend against the rest
Hannibal is confident of easy success and promises a great reward for taking or killing Eumenes

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s trick with the messenger entertaining for the reader?
points: the trick takes place in the tense moment before the signal for battle
the reader is told the messenger’s real purpose before the enemy can guess it
the messenger looks harmless and official, with a small boat and a herald’s staff
the enemy assume the letter is about peace and take him straight to the king
his real task, pointing out the king’s ship, is done almost in passing, and he returns safely
the letter contains nothing but mockery, so Eumenes is humiliated before the battle
Eumenes is baffled yet rushes into battle, while the reader knows he is heading into a trap

essays.q: how does Nepos make the defeat of the Pergamene fleet dramatic?
points: Eumenes, Rome’s proud ally, is reduced to running away and only just escapes
the rest of the Pergamene fleet is winning, which makes the sudden reversal more striking
Nepos reminds the reader of the pots, so the reader knows their secret when the Pergamenes do not
the Pergamenes first laugh at the pots, and the laughter turns to terror
the shock of the snakes and the sailors’ confusion about which danger to avoid
their flight back to camp completes the rout
Nepos ends by praising Hannibal’s strategy, proving his genius on land as well as at sea

essays.q: how does Nepos build up a sense of danger around Hannibal?
points: Flamininus wastes no time and reports the news the next day
the senate thinks Rome will never be safe while Hannibal is alive, which shows how much he is still feared
an embassy including Flamininus is sent to demand that Hannibal be handed over
Prusias is too afraid of Rome to refuse
he hides behind the law of hospitality while telling the Romans they can find Hannibal easily
Hannibal has prepared for this moment by building exits on every side of his house
quod accidit tells the reader that the moment he feared has come, creating suspense

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s last moments dramatic?
points: the house is surrounded by a large force of armed men
the scene is seen through the eyes of a slave boy at the door, which makes it small and personal
Hannibal stays calm and practical, sending the boy round every door
the exits he built so carefully are all blocked
he sees at once that he is being hunted and that this is no accident
he chooses to die by his own hand rather than at the will of his enemies
he acts in keeping with his past courage, and the narrative ends on his taking the poison

essays.lemma: puer cum celeriter … M. Baebio Tamphilo
essays.q: how does Nepos bring the Life of Hannibal to a fitting close?
points: Hannibal understands his position at once and reaches his decision calmly
he keeps control by choosing the manner of his own death
his suicide is presented as worthy of his past courage, a noble death
the poison he always kept with him shows his foresight to the very end
Nepos gives a final verdict of the highest praise, ‘the bravest of men’
his death is described gently as a rest after a life of many hardships
Nepos ends as a careful scholar, setting out the different dates his sources give
